title: ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity
tagline: Entry-level cybersecurity foundations across the five official CC domains: security principles, continuity and incident response, access control, network security, and security operations.
disclaimer: Independent training material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ISC2. This material confers no certification and is not a substitute for official ISC2 training. All scenarios and questions are original practice content; no exam content is reproduced.

domains.name: Security Principles
domains.summary: The CIA triad, risk management concepts and calculations, types of security controls, and governance including policies, data classification, and professional ethics.

scenarios.title: The Altered Ledger
scenarios.situation: A junior accountant at a regional bank notices the quarterly close spreadsheet totals differ from the values the finance system exported the day before. The audit trail shows a staff member with edit rights changed several cells overnight to "round" the numbers before a board presentation. Nothing was copied or deleted, and everyone who needed the file could still open it.
evidence: The CIA triad

Confidentiality means only authorized parties can access data. Integrity means data is accurate and is altered only by authorized actions. Availability means data and systems are accessible when needed.
Audit trail finding
The exported values were modified after export by an unauthorized change. No access outage occurred, and no outsider viewed the file.
choices: Confidentiality — the data was exposed to the wrong people
Integrity — the data was altered without authorization
Availability — the data could not be reached
Accountability — the data was never logged
scenarios.why: The numbers were changed without authorization, which is the textbook definition of an integrity violation: data must remain accurate and be modified only through authorized actions. Confidentiality was not breached (nobody unauthorized read it), availability was unaffected (the file stayed reachable), and accountability is a supporting concept, not the violated principle.
scenarios.hint: Ask what happened to the data itself — was it read by the wrong eyes, changed without permission, or blocked from its users?
objectives: Define the CIA triad
Map a real incident to confidentiality, integrity, or availability

scenarios.title: The $12,000 Question
scenarios.situation: A risk assessment finds the customer database would cost $40,000 per breach to remediate (SLE). Ransomware is estimated to strike once every two years (ARO of 0.5), giving an annualized loss expectancy (ALE) of $20,000. A proposed immutable-backup control costs $12,000 per year and would cut the ARO to 0.1.
scenarios.prompt: Is the control cost-justified, and why?
evidence: Quantitative risk formulas
ALE = SLE x ARO. A control is cost-effective when the reduction in ALE it produces exceeds the control's annual cost. Risk can be reduced, transferred, accepted, or avoided — never fully eliminated.
The numbers
Current ALE: $40,000 x 0.5 = $20,000 per year. With the control: $40,000 x 0.1 = $4,000 per year. ALE reduction: $16,000 per year, versus a control cost of $12,000 per year.
choices: No — the control costs more than the asset is worth
Yes — the $16,000 ALE reduction exceeds the $12,000 annual cost
No — risk can never be reduced below the single loss expectancy
Yes — any control that lowers the ARO is automatically justified
scenarios.why: The control reduces expected annual loss by $16,000 at a cost of $12,000, a net benefit of $4,000 per year. Residual risk of $4,000 per year remains, which management may accept, transfer, or reduce further — but the control itself is a sound investment.
scenarios.hint: Compute the ALE with and without the control first, then compare the difference against the price tag.
objectives: Calculate ALE from SLE and ARO
Apply cost-benefit analysis to a control decision

scenarios.title: Layers at the Loading Dock
scenarios.situation: A data center has suffered two tailgating incidents this quarter. The security manager proposes three measures: (a) a mantrap with badge readers at the entrance, (b) CCTV cameras covering the loading dock, and (c) a written visitor-escort policy with a sign-in log.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement best describes this control set?
evidence: Control categories

Preventive controls stop incidents before they happen; detective controls identify them during or after the fact; corrective controls restore normal operations. Physical controls use tangible barriers and devices; administrative controls use policies, procedures, and training; technical (logical) controls use hardware or software mechanisms.
Defense in depth

Defense in depth layers multiple controls so that if one fails, others still protect the asset. Strong designs mix preventive, detective, and corrective controls across physical, administrative, and technical categories.
choices: All three are preventive physical controls, which is sufficient defense in depth
The mantrap is a preventive physical control, the CCTV is a detective physical control, and the visitor policy is an administrative control — together they form layered defense in depth
The visitor policy is a technical control and the CCTV is a preventive control
Tailgating is a technical attack, so only technical controls can address it
scenarios.why: The mantrap prevents unauthorized entry (preventive, physical), the CCTV records what happens for later review (detective, physical), and the escort policy governs human behavior (administrative). Layering different control functions and categories is exactly what defense in depth means; a single category alone would leave gaps.
scenarios.hint: Classify each item twice — by when it acts (before, during/after) and by what form it takes (barrier, device, or written rule).
objectives: Classify controls by function and category
Explain defense in depth

domains.name: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Incident Response
domains.summary: BCP and DRP fundamentals, business impact analysis with RTO and RPO, backup types and strategies, recovery site options, and the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle.

scenarios.title: Isolate First
scenarios.situation: Monday, 8:04 AM: the help desk receives three tickets about workstations running slowly, and each shows a ransom note on the desktop. The incident response playbook is open on the analyst's screen. The analyst's first move is to disconnect the affected machines from the network before doing anything else.
scenarios.prompt: Which NIST SP 800-61 incident response phase does this action belong to?
evidence: NIST SP 800-61 phases
Phase 1: Preparation. Phase 2: Detection and Analysis. Phase 3: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery. Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity (including lessons learned).
What just happened
The incident has already been detected — ransom notes and help desk tickets confirm it. Disconnecting machines limits the spread, which is a containment action, not preparation or analysis.
choices: Preparation — the team is getting ready to respond
Detection and Analysis — identifying what happened
Containment, Eradication, and Recovery — limiting the blast radius
Post-Incident Activity — writing the lessons-learned report
scenarios.why: Detection already occurred via the ransom notes and tickets, so the response has moved to phase 3. Isolating hosts stops the ransomware from reaching more machines — the defining goal of containment, which precedes eradication (removing the malware) and recovery (restoring systems).
scenarios.hint: The ransom notes mean detection is finished. What does unplugging the machines accomplish?
objectives: List the four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases
Place a response action in the correct phase

scenarios.title: Sunday Full, Wednesday Worry
scenarios.situation: A small firm runs a full backup every Sunday night. On Wednesday at noon the file server dies. Two weekday schemes are under consideration going forward. Scheme A takes incremental backups on Monday and Tuesday. Scheme B takes differential backups on Monday and Tuesday.
scenarios.prompt: Which scheme restores faster on Wednesday, and what is the trade-off?
evidence: Backup types

Full: copies everything. Incremental: copies changes since the last backup of any kind — fast to back up, slow to restore because the restore needs the full plus every incremental in sequence. Differential: copies changes since the last full backup — slower to back up than incremental, faster to restore because the restore needs only the full plus the latest differential.
The scenario
A Sunday full backup exists in both schemes. A Wednesday restore must replay the weekday sets on top of it.
choices: Incremental — a Wednesday restore needs only the full plus Tuesday's incremental
Differential — a Wednesday restore needs only the full plus Tuesday's differential, at the cost of larger weekday backups
Incremental restores faster because each individual backup file is smaller
Both schemes restore identically; the difference is only in backup speed
scenarios.why: A differential restore replays two sets (Sunday full + Tuesday differential), while an incremental restore replays three (Sunday full + Monday + Tuesday incrementals). The trade-off is that each differential grows larger through the week since it always reaches back to Sunday, consuming more backup time and media.
scenarios.hint: Count how many backup sets each Wednesday restore must replay in order.
objectives: Compare full, incremental, and differential backups
Choose a backup scheme for a restore-time requirement

scenarios.title: Four Hours Down, One Hour Lost
scenarios.situation: A business impact analysis (BIA) for the order-processing system finds two hard limits: the business can survive at most 4 hours of outage before losing key customers, and it can afford to lose at most 1 hour of transaction data. The disaster recovery team must set the RTO and RPO and choose a backup cadence.
scenarios.prompt: Which RTO/RPO pair matches the BIA, and what backup frequency does the RPO demand?
evidence: RTO vs RPO

RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum tolerable downtime — how fast systems must be back. RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum tolerable data loss, measured in time — it drives how frequently backups must run. Both derive from the BIA, which also identifies the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD).
BIA findings
Outage tolerance: 4 hours. Data-loss tolerance: 1 hour of transactions.
choices: RTO 1 hour, RPO 4 hours — back up every 4 hours
RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour — back up at least hourly
RTO 1 hour, RPO 1 hour — only continuous replication qualifies
RTO 4 hours, RPO 4 hours — back up every 4 hours
scenarios.why: The 4-hour outage tolerance sets the RTO at 4 hours; the 1-hour data-loss tolerance sets the RPO at 1 hour. An RPO of 1 hour means a backup (or replication point) must exist at least every hour, otherwise more than an hour of transactions could be lost.
scenarios.hint: RTO answers 'how long can we be down'; RPO answers 'how much data can we afford to lose'.
objectives: Distinguish RTO from RPO
Derive backup frequency from an RPO

domains.name: Access Control Concepts
domains.summary: Identification, authentication, authorization and accountability; authentication factors and MFA; authentication protocols; DAC, MAC, RBAC and ABAC models; and physical access controls.

scenarios.title: Two Proofs at the Door
scenarios.situation: A new payroll portal requires users to enter a password and then approve a push notification on their phone before they are signed in. The help desk confirms that a stolen password alone is no longer enough to access anyone's pay stubs.
scenarios.prompt: What authentication concept does this login flow implement?
evidence: Authentication factors

Something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone, hardware token, smart card), something you are (fingerprint, face, voice). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more factors from different categories.
The login flow
The password is something you know. Approving the push on the phone proves possession of something you have. Two distinct factor categories are in play.
choices: Single-factor authentication — the phone merely confirms the password
Multi-factor authentication — two different factor categories are required
Single sign-on — one login now works for many applications
Biometric authentication — the phone scans the user's face
scenarios.why: A password (know) plus phone approval (have) spans two factor categories, which is the definition of MFA. It is not single sign-on (no cross-application federation is described) and no biometric is involved.
scenarios.hint: Count the factor categories, not the number of steps on the screen.
objectives: Name the three authentication factor categories
Recognize MFA versus single-factor authentication

scenarios.title: Labels on Everything
scenarios.situation: A defense contractor's file server tags every document with a classification label (Unclassified, Confidential, or Secret) and every user carries a clearance level. The system grants access only when the user's clearance dominates the document's label, and file owners cannot share documents at their own discretion even with other cleared staff.
scenarios.prompt: Which access control model is this?
evidence: Access control models

DAC (discretionary): the data owner decides who gets access, e.g., setting file permissions. MAC (mandatory): the system enforces access based on security labels and clearances; users cannot override it. RBAC (role-based): access follows the user's job role. ABAC (attribute-based): access follows evaluated attributes of user, resource, and environment.
The system's rule
Labels plus clearances are enforced by the system itself, with no owner discretion — the defining trait of MAC.
choices: Discretionary access control (DAC)
Mandatory access control (MAC)
Role-based access control (RBAC)
Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
scenarios.why: System-enforced security labels and clearances that users cannot override are the hallmark of mandatory access control, commonly used in government and military environments. DAC would let owners share freely, and RBAC would key off job roles rather than labels.
scenarios.hint: Who decides — the file owner, the job role, or the system's labels?
objectives: Differentiate DAC, MAC, RBAC, and ABAC
Match a labeled, clearance-based environment to MAC

scenarios.title: One Login for Five Partners
scenarios.situation: A manufacturer wants its engineers to sign in once with the corporate identity provider and then open a partner company's web-based CAD portal without a second login. The partner must trust the manufacturer's authentication rather than maintaining its own passwords for these engineers.
scenarios.prompt: Which protocol is the standard fit for this federated web single sign-on?
evidence: Federation and AAA protocols

SAML 2.0 is the XML-based standard for federated SSO to web applications: an identity provider sends signed assertions about the user to a service provider. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization/delegation framework (often paired with OpenID Connect for authentication), common for APIs and mobile apps. Kerberos is a ticket-based protocol for LAN authentication. RADIUS and TACACS+ centralize authentication, authorization, and accounting for network devices.
The requirement
Browser-based SSO across organizational boundaries, where the partner trusts identity assertions from the manufacturer's identity provider.
choices: Kerberos — issue service tickets across the public internet
SAML 2.0 — federated SSO with identity provider assertions
RADIUS — centralize the partner's remote-access logins
TACACS+ — authorize each CAD command individually
scenarios.why: SAML 2.0 was built for exactly this: cross-organization, browser-based SSO via trusted assertions from an identity provider. Kerberos is LAN-oriented, RADIUS/TACACS+ target network-device AAA, and OAuth 2.0 is primarily an API delegation framework rather than the classic enterprise web-SSO standard.
scenarios.hint: Think 'web browser plus another company trusting your login' — which standard was designed for that exchange?
objectives: Compare SAML, OAuth/OIDC, Kerberos, and RADIUS/TACACS+
Select SAML for federated web SSO

domains.name: Network Security
domains.summary: OSI model security threats by layer, network segmentation and DMZ design, firewall and IDS/IPS concepts, VPN types, and wireless security including WPA3 and rogue access points.

scenarios.title: Where Does the Web Server Live?
scenarios.situation: A company hosts a public web server that customers reach over the internet, plus an internal database holding customer records that must never be directly reachable from outside. A firewall separates the network zones.
evidence: Segmentation basics

A DMZ (demilitarized zone) is a screened subnet between the internet and the internal network, used for public-facing services. Sensitive internal systems stay on the protected internal network, and the firewall controls traffic between the zones.
The two systems
The web server must be reachable from the internet; the database must not be.
choices: Both on the internal network — a single firewall is enough
Web server in the DMZ, database on the internal network
Database in the DMZ, web server on the internal network
Both in the DMZ for equal protection
scenarios.why: The public-facing web server belongs in the DMZ where internet clients can reach it without touching the internal network, while the database stays protected inside. The firewall mediates the web server's limited, necessary queries to the database.
scenarios.hint: Which system must the internet touch directly, and which must it never touch?
objectives: Explain the purpose of a DMZ
Place public and internal systems in the correct zones

scenarios.title: Free_WiFi in the Lobby
scenarios.situation: Employees report a new open network named "CorpWiFi" appearing in the lobby. The real corporate SSID uses WPA3-Enterprise with certificates. Several laptops auto-connected to the imposter and were served a fake login page that harvested their credentials.
scenarios.prompt: What attack is this, and what is the strongest mitigation?
evidence: Wireless attacks

An evil twin is a rogue access point impersonating a legitimate SSID to intercept traffic or harvest credentials. WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X provides mutual authentication: the client verifies the network's certificate before sending credentials, which defeats impersonation. A wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) detects rogue access points.
What happened
An imposter SSID plus a credential-harvesting portal is the classic evil twin pattern, and auto-connect made the exposure worse.
choices: A deauthentication attack — hide the SSID to fix it
An evil twin — enforce WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X mutual authentication and deploy a WIPS to detect rogues
A SYN flood — block ICMP at the firewall
MAC spoofing — it cannot be mitigated
scenarios.why: Copying the corporate SSID to harvest credentials is an evil twin attack. Mutual authentication means the laptop validates the network's certificate before transmitting credentials, so the imposter fails validation; a WIPS adds detection of the rogue radio. Hiding the SSID is weak security through obscurity.
scenarios.hint: The attacker copied the network's name — how can a laptop prove the network is genuine before sending credentials?
objectives: Identify an evil twin attack
Apply WPA3-Enterprise, 802.1X, and WIPS as mitigations

scenarios.title: Poisoned ARP Tables
scenarios.situation: The SOC sees a flood of gratuitous ARP replies mapping the gateway's IP address to an unknown MAC address. Workstations' ARP caches now point at the attacker's machine, and login traffic is being relayed through it to the real gateway.
scenarios.prompt: At which OSI layer is this attack operating, and what is it enabling?
evidence: ARP and the OSI model

ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses and operates at the Data Link layer (Layer 2). Forged ARP replies (ARP spoofing or poisoning) let an attacker impersonate the gateway, placing the attacker in a classic man-in-the-middle position.
Observed effects
The gateway's IP is now bound to the attacker's MAC, and traffic is being relayed through the attacker — the signature of interception, not flooding or redirection at higher layers.
choices: Layer 3 — IP spoofing enabling a denial-of-service attack
Layer 2 — ARP spoofing enabling a man-in-the-middle attack
Layer 4 — a SYN flood exhausting the gateway
Layer 7 — DNS poisoning redirecting web traffic
scenarios.why: ARP is a Layer 2 protocol, and poisoning ARP caches to impersonate the gateway puts the attacker between the victims and their traffic — a man-in-the-middle. No flooding (DoS) or name-resolution (DNS) behavior is present.
scenarios.hint: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses — which layer speaks in MAC addresses?
objectives: Map common attacks to OSI layers
Explain how ARP spoofing enables a man-in-the-middle

domains.name: Security Operations
domains.summary: Logging and monitoring with SIEM, cryptography fundamentals (symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, PKI), malware types, system hardening, and social engineering awareness.

scenarios.title: It Spread Without a Click
scenarios.situation: Overnight, malware hopped from one unpatched workstation to file shares across the whole subnet. Nobody opened an attachment or ran a program — the malware exploited a network service vulnerability to copy itself from machine to machine.
scenarios.prompt: What type of malware is this?
evidence: Malware types

Virus: attaches to a host file and needs user action to spread. Worm: self-replicating across networks without user action. Trojan: disguised as legitimate software; does not self-replicate. Ransomware: encrypts data and demands payment — a payload, not a propagation method.
Observed behavior
No user action occurred, yet the malware copied itself across the network by exploiting a service vulnerability.
choices: Virus — it infected host files on each machine
Worm — self-replicating with no user action required
Trojan — it posed as a legitimate software update
Rootkit — it hid in the boot sector
scenarios.why: Self-propagation across the network with zero user interaction is the defining trait of a worm. A virus would need a host file and someone to execute it, and a trojan relies on tricking the user rather than copying itself.
scenarios.hint: What spread it — a person clicking something, or the malware copying itself?
objectives: Distinguish virus, worm, and trojan
Identify worm behavior in an incident

scenarios.title: Sealed and Signed
scenarios.situation: The legal department must email a signed contract to external counsel. Two requirements: only the counsel can read it, and the counsel must be able to prove it genuinely came from Legal and arrived unaltered.
scenarios.prompt: Which cryptographic combination meets both requirements?
evidence: Asymmetric cryptography basics

Encrypting with the recipient's public key means only the recipient's private key can decrypt it (confidentiality). Signing means encrypting a hash of the message with the sender's private key; anyone can verify it with the sender's public key (authenticity and integrity).
The two requirements
Readable only by counsel means confidentiality. Provably from Legal and unaltered means authenticity plus integrity.
choices: Encrypt with Legal's private key and send the hash in plaintext
Encrypt with the counsel's public key and sign with Legal's private key
Hash the contract and email only the hash
Encrypt with a shared password posted on the intranet
scenarios.why: The counsel's public key provides confidentiality (only their private key opens it), and Legal's private-key signature provides authenticity and integrity (only Legal could have signed it, and any alteration breaks verification). Each key is used for the job it was designed for.
scenarios.hint: Whose public key locks the message, and whose private key signs it?
objectives: Apply public/private key roles for confidentiality and signing
Combine encryption and digital signatures

scenarios.title: 4,000 Failures, Then Success
scenarios.situation: The SIEM correlates overnight logs: 4,000 failed logins against the svc-backup account from IP addresses in three countries, then one success from a new foreign IP, followed by large outbound data transfers. The account has no MFA enrolled.
scenarios.prompt: What does the correlation indicate, and what is the priority response?
evidence: SIEM correlation

A SIEM aggregates logs from many sources and correlates events into timelines. Thousands of failures followed by a single success is the classic signature of a successful brute-force or password-spray attack; the outbound transfers that follow suggest data exfiltration.
Account facts
A service account with no MFA is now authenticating from an anomalous foreign IP and moving large volumes of data out.
choices: Normal administrator activity — whitelist the foreign IP
A successful brute-force attack — disable and reset the account, block the IPs, investigate the exfiltration, and enforce MFA
A SIEM misconfiguration — tune the rule and move on
A denial-of-service attack — engage the ISP for traffic scrubbing
scenarios.why: The failures-then-success pattern proves the password was guessed, and the egress indicates the attacker is now stealing data. Containment comes first: disable and reset the compromised account, block attacker infrastructure, determine what was taken, and close the gap with MFA — in that priority order.
scenarios.hint: What story do failures, then success, then uploads tell when read as one timeline?
objectives: Interpret correlated SIEM events
Prioritize containment for a compromised account

lessons.title: Security Principles: CIA, Risk, Controls, and Governance
concepts: The CIA triad is the foundation of all security thinking. Confidentiality ensures only authorized parties can access data — achieved through encryption, access controls, and classification. Integrity ensures data is accurate and is changed only by authorized actions — achieved through hashing, checksums, digital signatures, and change control. Availability ensures data and systems are reachable when needed — achieved through redundancy, backups, patching, and denial-of-service defenses. Nearly every exam question about 'which principle' maps to one of these three.

Risk is the combination of a threat (anything that could cause harm, such as ransomware) and a vulnerability (a weakness the threat can exploit, such as unpatched software). Formally, risk exists where a threat meets a vulnerability and an asset is exposed. Qualitative risk analysis ranks risks with labels like high/medium/low; quantitative analysis uses numbers: single loss expectancy (SLE) is the cost of one incident, annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is how often it is expected per year, and annualized loss expectancy (ALE) equals SLE times ARO. Controls are judged by comparing their cost against the ALE reduction they deliver.

Security controls are described two ways. By function: preventive controls stop incidents (firewalls, mantraps, least privilege), detective controls spot them (IDS, CCTV, log monitoring), corrective controls restore normal operations (backups, incident response), deterrent controls discourage attackers (warning banners, visible guards), and compensating controls substitute when the ideal control is impractical. By category: administrative controls are policies and procedures, technical (logical) controls are hardware and software mechanisms, and physical controls are tangible barriers and devices. Defense in depth layers controls across both dimensions so no single failure is fatal.

Governance turns security intent into organizational reality. Policies are high-level statements of management intent; standards mandate specific technologies or configurations; procedures are step-by-step instructions; guidelines are recommended (not mandatory) best practices; baselines define minimum security configurations. Data classification (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) drives handling rules, with data owners deciding classification, custodians implementing protections, and users following the rules.

Professional ethics matter at the entry level too. The ISC2 Code of Ethics binds members to four canons: protect society, the commonwealth, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession. When a scenario pits convenience against integrity, the ethical answer follows these canons.

example.code:
# Quantitative risk: is a $12,000/year control worth it?
SLE=40000        # cost of one breach
ARO_BEFORE=0.5   # once every two years
ARO_AFTER=0.1    # with the control
COST=12000

ALE_BEFORE=$(echo "$SLE * $ARO_BEFORE" | bc)
ALE_AFTER=$(echo "$SLE * $ARO_AFTER" | bc)
SAVINGS=$(echo "$ALE_BEFORE - $ALE_AFTER" | bc)

echo "ALE before: \$$ALE_BEFORE /yr"
echo "ALE after:  \$$ALE_AFTER /yr"
echo "Savings:    \$$SAVINGS /yr vs cost \$$COST /yr"
if [ "$SAVINGS" -gt "$COST" ]; then
  echo "Decision: IMPLEMENT (savings exceed cost)"
else
  echo "Decision: REJECT (cost exceeds savings)"
fi
example.walkthrough: This script implements the ALE = SLE x ARO formula from the lesson. It computes the annualized loss expectancy before the control ($20,000) and after ($4,000), derives the $16,000 yearly savings, and compares it to the $12,000 control cost. Because savings exceed cost, the control is cost-justified — the same arithmetic behind scenario isc2-cc-sc2. Notice the script never claims risk reaches zero: a residual ALE of $4,000 remains for management to accept, transfer, or reduce further.

pitfalls: Encryption protects confidentiality, not integrity — an encrypted file can still be corrupted; integrity needs hashing or signatures.
Risk can be reduced, transferred (insurance), accepted, or avoided — but never eliminated entirely.
Deterrent is not the same as preventive: a warning banner discourages but does not block, while a firewall blocks.
Policies state intent; procedures give steps. Mixing them up is a classic exam trap.
lessons.try_it: Walk through your home setup and name one preventive, one detective, and one corrective control you already have (for example: a door lock, a smoke detector, and a backup drive). Then classify each as administrative, technical, or physical.

lessons.title: Continuity, Recovery, and Incident Response
concepts: Business continuity planning (BCP) keeps the business operating during a disruption; disaster recovery planning (DRP) restores IT systems afterward. The business impact analysis (BIA) is the foundation of both: it identifies critical processes, their dependencies, and how much pain an outage causes. From the BIA come the recovery targets: the recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum tolerable downtime, the recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, and the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is the absolute limit before the business faces existential harm. RTO must never exceed MTD, and RPO drives backup frequency.

Backups are the core corrective control. A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies changes since the last backup of any kind (fast to take, slow to restore — you need the full plus every incremental); a differential backup copies changes since the last full (slower to take than incremental, faster to restore — you need only the full plus the latest differential). The widely cited 3-2-1 rule keeps three copies of data on two different media with one copy offsite. Backups must be tested — an untested backup is a hope, not a control — and at least one copy should be offline or immutable so ransomware cannot encrypt it.

Recovery sites come in three flavors. A hot site is fully equipped and can take over in hours but costs the most. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs configuration, taking days. A cold site is just space and power, taking weeks but costing the least. The choice follows the RTO: the shorter the RTO, the hotter (and pricier) the site. Reciprocal agreements, where two organizations host each other's recovery capability, are a budget alternative.

Incident response follows NIST Special Publication 800-61's four-phase lifecycle. Preparation builds the team, tools, playbooks, and communication plans before anything happens. Detection and Analysis identifies and triages potential incidents using alerts, logs, and user reports. Containment, Eradication, and Recovery limits the blast radius, removes the cause, and restores systems to normal. Post-Incident Activity captures lessons learned and feeds improvements back into preparation. Skipping straight to recovery without containment and eradication is how incidents recur.

Communication discipline matters during incidents: know who declares an incident, who talks to executives, legal, and regulators, and what gets documented for the post-incident review. Evidence handling — preserving logs and forensic images with a documented chain of custody — keeps response options (including legal ones) open.

example.code:
INCIDENT: Ransomware notes on 3 workstations, 08:04 Monday

Phase 1 - Preparation (already done before the incident):
  IR team roster, playbook, and call tree existed; backups
  were tested last month; an offline backup copy is available.

Phase 2 - Detection and Analysis:
  08:04  Help desk tickets + ransom notes = confirmed incident
  08:15  Analyst scopes: 3 hosts, same subnet, same file share

Phase 3 - Containment, Eradication, and Recovery:
  08:20  CONTAIN: disconnect the 3 hosts from the network
  09:00  ERADICATE: reimage hosts from known-good media
  10:30  RECOVER: restore file share from offline backup,
           verify hashes, return to service

Phase 4 - Post-Incident Activity:
  Root cause: unpatched SMB service. Actions: emergency
  patching, network segmentation for the subnet, phishing
  refresher, playbook update. Lessons-learned report filed.
example.walkthrough: This walkthrough applies the NIST 800-61 lifecycle to the ransomware scenario from isc2-cc-sc4. Note the ordering discipline: containment (isolate) comes before eradication (reimage), which comes before recovery (restore) — restoring before eradicating would just re-infect the systems. Preparation done earlier (tested, offline backups) is what makes the recovery phase possible at all. The post-incident phase converts the pain into durable improvements, closing the loop back to preparation.

pitfalls: Restoring from backup before eradicating the malware re-infects the systems — containment and eradication come first.
Confusing RTO (how fast to recover) with RPO (how much data you can lose) — RPO drives backup frequency, RTO drives recovery-site choice.
Incremental restores need the full plus EVERY incremental in sequence; forgetting one breaks the chain.
An untested backup is not a control. Test restores on a schedule and document the results.
lessons.try_it: Write a one-page incident playbook for 'laptop stolen from a car': list your detection step, your containment step, your eradication/recovery steps, and two lessons-learned actions. Time yourself — playbooks are written before the incident, not during it.

lessons.title: Access Control: IAAA, MFA, Protocols, and Models
concepts: Access control runs on IAAA: Identification (claiming an identity, e.g., typing a username), Authentication (proving it, e.g., entering a password), Authorization (what the proven identity is allowed to do), and Accountability (logging actions so they can be traced to the identity). Authentication must precede authorization — the system cannot decide what you may do until it knows who you are — and accountability depends on the logs capturing all of it.

Authentication factors come in three categories: something you know (passwords, PINs), something you have (phones, hardware tokens, smart cards), and something you are (fingerprints, face, voice). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more factors from different categories; two steps within the same category (password plus security question) is still single-factor. Biometrics are convenient but irrevocable — you cannot reissue a fingerprint — so they are best paired with another factor and protected accordingly.

Common authentication protocols each have a home turf. Kerberos is the ticket-based LAN standard (used by Active Directory). LDAP (often LDAPS) provides directory lookups for identity data. RADIUS and TACACS+ centralize AAA for network devices, with TACACS+ separating authentication, authorization, and accounting and encrypting the full payload. SAML 2.0 is the XML standard for federated web single sign-on via identity-provider assertions. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization/delegation framework — often paired with OpenID Connect for authentication — dominant in APIs and mobile apps. CHAP and PAP are legacy PPP authentication protocols; EAP frameworks underpin WPA-Enterprise wireless authentication.

Authorization models decide who gets what. DAC (discretionary) lets data owners grant access at their discretion, as with file ACLs. MAC (mandatory) has the system enforce access from security labels and clearances that users cannot override — the government and military model. RBAC (role-based) assigns permissions to job roles and users to roles, simplifying administration and supporting least privilege. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates attributes of the subject, resource, action, and environment for fine-grained, context-aware decisions. Rule-based access control applies global rules (such as time-of-day restrictions) uniformly.

Account management and physical controls complete the picture. Provisioning grants access on hire or role change, deprovisioning revokes it promptly on departure — orphaned accounts are a classic attack path. Least privilege gives users only the access their role requires, enforced through periodic access reviews and separation of duties for sensitive processes. Physical controls — mantraps, badge readers, biometrics, CCTV, bollards, cable locks, visitor logs — protect the facilities where the technical controls live.

example.code:
DECISION: partner engineers need web-portal access

Requirement: sign in once with the corporate identity
provider, then use the partner's browser-based CAD portal
with no second login. The partner must trust our
authentication.

Candidate protocols:
  Kerberos .... LAN ticket system; does not cross the
                public internet to another organization.
  RADIUS ...... AAA for network devices, not browser SSO.
  OAuth 2.0 ... delegation for APIs/mobile apps; the
                classic enterprise web-SSO standard is older.
  SAML 2.0 .... XML assertions from an identity provider
                to a service provider; built for federated
                browser SSO.

Choice: SAML 2.0. The corporate IdP issues signed
assertions; the partner's portal (service provider)
validates them and creates the session. No partner-side
passwords to manage, and deprovisioning at the IdP
instantly cuts partner access too.
example.walkthrough: This is the reasoning behind scenario isc2-cc-sc9. The key discriminator is 'browser-based SSO across organizational boundaries' — that phrase points to federation, and the enterprise federation standard is SAML 2.0. OAuth 2.0 plus OpenID Connect is the modern alternative many SaaS apps use, but SAML remains the canonical answer for cross-company web SSO. Note the operational bonus: centralizing authentication at the identity provider means one deprovisioning action revokes access everywhere.

pitfalls: Two steps are not automatically MFA — a password plus a security question is still one factor (something you know).
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. SSO authenticates once — it does not grant universal authorization.
SSO is convenient but a single point of failure: protect the identity provider with MFA and monitor it closely.
Biometrics identify but cannot be revoked — never use them as the sole factor for high-value access.
lessons.try_it: List every account you own that protects money or identity. Mark which have MFA enabled and which factor types they use. Enable MFA (preferably an authenticator app or hardware key over SMS) on any that lack it.

lessons.title: Network Security: Layers, Segmentation, and Wireless
concepts: The OSI model gives every attack an address. Layer 1 (Physical): wiretaps, signal jamming. Layer 2 (Data Link): MAC flooding, ARP spoofing/poisoning. Layer 3 (Network): IP spoofing, ICMP attacks, rogue routing. Layer 4 (Transport): SYN floods, port scanning, session hijacking at the TCP level. Layer 5 (Session): session hijacking and fixation. Layer 6 (Presentation): SSL/TLS stripping and encryption abuse. Layer 7 (Application): phishing, SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), DNS poisoning, and malware delivery. Mapping an attack to its layer immediately suggests the right control.

Segmentation limits blast radius. VLANs separate broadcast domains at Layer 2; subnetting separates them at Layer 3; a DMZ (demilitarized zone) is a screened subnet for public-facing services between the internet and the internal network; microsegmentation applies fine-grained policy around individual workloads. The design rule is simple: internet-facing services live in the DMZ, sensitive data lives inside, and firewalls enforce least-privilege traffic between zones.

Firewalls and intrusion systems are complementary, not interchangeable. Packet-filtering firewalls judge individual packets by header fields; stateful firewalls track connection state; next-generation firewalls (NGFW) add application awareness, user identity, and threat intelligence. An IDS (intrusion detection system) watches and alerts — passive, usually placed to monitor traffic via a span port or tap. An IPS (intrusion prevention system) sits inline and can block — active, but a misconfigured IPS can break legitimate traffic. Honeypots and honeynets are decoy systems that attract attackers and generate high-fidelity alerts.

VPNs extend private networks across untrusted ones. Site-to-site VPNs connect whole networks (branch to headquarters), typically with IPsec. Remote-access VPNs connect individual users, commonly with IPsec or TLS/SSL VPNs. IPsec operates at the network layer and offers tunnel mode (gateway to gateway) and transport mode (host to host), with AH providing integrity and ESP providing confidentiality plus integrity. TLS VPNs work through the browser or a lightweight client and traverse NAT and restrictive firewalls more easily.

Wireless security has evolved hard lessons. WEP is broken and must never be used; WPA2 (AES-CCMP) was the long standard; WPA3 is current, adding stronger handshakes (SAE) and forward secrecy, with WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X and certificates for mutual authentication. Threats include rogue access points, evil twins (impersonating the legitimate SSID to harvest credentials), deauthentication attacks, and wardriving. Mitigations: WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, a wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) to find rogues, and disabling auto-connect on managed devices.

example.code:
# Reviewing a firewall ruleset for dangerous permits
$ cat fw-rules.txt
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3389 -s 0.0.0.0/0 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -j DROP

# Which services are exposed, and to whom?
$ grep ACCEPT fw-rules.txt | awk '{print $4, $6, $8}'
--dport 22 -s 10.0.0.0/8     # SSH: internal only. OK.
--dport 80                  # HTTP: open to the world. Expected for a web server.
--dport 443                 # HTTPS: open to the world. Expected.
--dport 23                  # TELNET: open to the world. FINDING!
--dport 3389 -s 0.0.0.0/0   # RDP: open to the world. FINDING!

# Findings: Telnet (23) sends credentials in cleartext and
# should be disabled; RDP (3389) exposed to 0.0.0.0/0 invites
# brute force. Remediation: remove the Telnet rule, restrict
# RDP to the management subnet or require VPN + MFA.
example.walkthrough: This example shows the core network-security review skill: read the ruleset, map each permitted port to a service and a source, and flag violations of least privilege. Telnet is the louder finding because it transmits credentials in cleartext (a confidentiality failure at Layer 7 riding on Layer 4). RDP open to the world is the classic brute-force target seen in scenario isc2-cc-sc15's SIEM pattern. The final default-DROP rule is the correct posture: deny everything not explicitly permitted.

pitfalls: An IDS detects and alerts; only an IPS can block. Placing an IDS inline expecting prevention is a design error.
NAT hides internal addresses but is not a security boundary — it was designed for address conservation.
Hiding the SSID or filtering MAC addresses is obscurity, not security; both are trivially bypassed.
WEP is cryptographically broken. Any question offering WEP as acceptable is a trap.
lessons.try_it: On your home router's admin page, check three things: is remote administration disabled on the WAN interface, is WPS turned off, and is the Wi-Fi using WPA2 or WPA3 (not WEP, not open)? Change anything that fails.

lessons.title: Security Operations: Logging, Crypto, Malware, and Hardening
concepts: Logging and monitoring turn noise into signal. Log authentication events, privilege use, system changes, and network connections; synchronize all clocks with NTP so timestamps correlate across systems; protect logs from tampering by forwarding them to a central, append-only store with restricted access; and retain them per policy and legal requirements. A SIEM (security and information event management) aggregates logs, normalizes them, correlates events into timelines, and raises alerts on defined rules — the '4,000 failures then one success' pattern from scenario isc2-cc-sc15 is exactly what correlation rules catch. SOAR platforms extend this by orchestrating automated response playbooks.

Cryptography provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. Symmetric encryption (one shared key, e.g., AES-256) is fast and suits bulk data. Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pairs, e.g., RSA, elliptic-curve ECC) solves key distribution and enables signatures but is slower. Hashing (e.g., SHA-256) is one-way: it produces a fixed-size digest for integrity checking but cannot be reversed — hashing is not encryption. HMAC combines a hash with a secret key for authenticated integrity. Digital signatures (hash encrypted with the sender's private key) prove authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation. PKI (public key infrastructure) with certificate authorities (CAs) binds public keys to identities, underpinning TLS. Key management — generation, distribution, rotation, and destruction — is where real-world crypto usually fails.

Malware comes in recognizable families. A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm self-replicates across networks without user action; a trojan masquerades as legitimate software; ransomware encrypts data and demands payment; spyware and keyloggers steal information silently; a rootkit buries itself to maintain privileged hidden access; a RAT (remote access trojan) gives attackers interactive control; logic bombs trigger on a condition. Defenses layer antivirus/EDR, patching, application allow-listing, email filtering, backups, and user awareness.

Hardening reduces attack surface before attacks arrive. Apply patches promptly, disable unnecessary services and ports, remove default credentials, enforce least privilege, configure baselines and audit against them, enable host firewalls with default-deny, encrypt data at rest and in transit, and deploy endpoint protection. Every open port and running service is a promise to defend — make fewer promises.

Social engineering bypasses technology by targeting people. Phishing is bulk fraudulent email; spear phishing targets specific individuals with researched lures; whaling targets executives; vishing uses voice calls; pretexting invents a scenario to extract information; baiting dangles something tempting (like an infected USB drive). Defenses: verify through independent channels, hover before clicking, report suspicious messages, and train continuously — the human is both the target and a sensor.

example.code:
# Integrity checking with SHA-256 hashes
$ printf 'Contract v3 - payment $50,000\n' > contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 8f3a...c41d

# The recipient recomputes the hash on arrival:
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 8f3a...c41d   # match -> unaltered

# Now simulate tampering in transit:
$ printf 'Contract v3 - payment $90,000\n' > contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 1b77...e902   # DIFFERENT -> tampered!

# A hash detects change but not the author. For proof of
# origin, the sender signs the hash with their private key:
$ openssl dgst -sha256 -sign legal.key -out contract.sig contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 -verify legal.pub -signature contract.sig contract.txt
Verified OK
example.walkthrough: This demonstrates the two halves of scenario isc2-cc-sc14. Hashing alone gives integrity: any alteration, even one character, produces a completely different digest (the avalanche effect), so the recipient detects tampering by recomputing. But a hash cannot prove who created the file — an attacker could alter the file and recompute the hash. The digital signature fixes that: only Legal's private key could have produced a signature that verifies with Legal's public key, delivering authenticity and non-repudiation on top of integrity.

pitfalls: Hashing is not encryption — a hash cannot be 'decrypted' back into the data, and it provides no confidentiality.
Encrypting with your own private key does not give confidentiality — anyone with your public key can read it; that operation is a signature.
Logs without synchronized time (NTP) cannot be correlated — timestamps become fiction across systems.
Security through obscurity (hidden SSIDs, secret algorithms) is not a control; Kerckhoffs's principle says the system must stay secure even when the design is public.
lessons.try_it: Pick any file on your computer and run `openssl dgst -sha256` (or `certutil -hashfile` on Windows / `shasum -a 256` on macOS) on it twice. Confirm the digests match, then change one byte and watch the digest change completely.

labs.title: Classify the Controls
labs.objective: Build a list of security controls in the terminal and classify each by function (preventive, detective, corrective) and category (physical, administrative, technical) using shell commands.
steps:
Create the control list: `printf 'mantrap
CCTV
backup
visitor-policy
firewall
' > controls.txt` and confirm with `cat controls.txt`.
Find the preventive physical control with `grep -i mantrap controls.txt` — a mantrap stops tailgating before it happens.
Find the detective control with `grep -i cctv controls.txt` — cameras record events for later review.
Find the corrective control with `grep -i backup controls.txt` — backups restore operations after an incident.
Classify the remaining two yourself: is the visitor-policy administrative or technical? Is the firewall preventive or detective?

checks.hint: Run grep for the mantrap entry: `grep -i mantrap controls.txt`.
Run grep for the CCTV entry: `grep -i cctv controls.txt`.
Run grep for the backup entry: `grep -i backup controls.txt`.

labs.title: Salt the Password Hash
labs.objective: Use openssl to hash a password with two different salts and observe why salting defeats rainbow-table attacks on stolen password databases.
steps: Hash a password with the first salt: `openssl passwd -6 -salt NaClSalt1 'S3cureP@ss'` and note the output starts with `$6$` (SHA-512 crypt).
Hash the SAME password with a different salt: `openssl passwd -6 -salt NaClSalt2 'S3cureP@ss'`.
Compare the two outputs: identical password, completely different hashes — the salt makes each hash unique.

Reflect: a rainbow table precomputes hashes for common passwords, but with a unique random salt per user the attacker must recompute the table for every salt — this is why modern systems salt (and pepper/stretch with bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2).

checks.hint: Hash a password with SHA-512 crypt: `openssl passwd -6 -salt <salt> '<password>'`. The output begins with $6$.

labs.title: Audit the Firewall Ruleset
labs.objective: Write a small firewall ruleset to a file, then use grep to find every permitted service and flag the rules that violate least privilege.
steps:
Create the ruleset: `printf 'ALLOW tcp 22 from 10.0.0.0/8
ALLOW tcp 80 from any
ALLOW tcp 443 from any
ALLOW tcp 23 from any
ALLOW tcp 3389 from any
DENY all
' > fw-rules.txt`.
List every permitted service: `grep ALLOW fw-rules.txt`.
Identify the dangerous findings: Telnet (port 23) transmits credentials in cleartext, and RDP (port 3389) open to `any` invites brute force.
State the remediation aloud: remove the Telnet rule entirely, and restrict RDP to the management subnet or require VPN plus MFA.

checks.hint: List the permitted rules with `grep ALLOW fw-rules.txt` and look for port 23 (Telnet).

labs.title: Prove the File Was Not Altered
labs.objective: Use SHA-256 hashing to detect tampering: hash a file, modify one byte, hash again, and observe the avalanche effect that underpins integrity controls.
steps: Create the file: `printf 'Contract v3 - payment 50000\n' > contract.txt`.
Record its digest: `openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt` — the output line begins with `SHA2-256(contract.txt)=`.
Tamper with one byte: `printf 'Contract v3 - payment 90000\n' > contract.txt`.
Hash again: `openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt` and compare — a completely different digest proves the file changed.
Connect the concept: this is exactly how file-integrity monitoring and signed software updates detect unauthorized modification.

checks.hint: Compute the file's SHA-256 digest: `openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt`.

sections.heading: Incident response — NIST SP 800-61 phases
items: 1. Preparation — team, tools, playbooks, communication plans, tested backups.
2. Detection and Analysis — triage alerts, logs, and user reports; scope the incident.
3. Containment, Eradication, and Recovery — isolate first, remove the cause, then restore.
4. Post-Incident Activity — root cause, lessons learned, playbook updates.
Order matters: never restore before eradicating, never eradicate before containing.

sections.heading: Access control models
items: DAC (discretionary) — data owners grant access at their discretion (file ACLs).
MAC (mandatory) — the system enforces labels and clearances; users cannot override (military/government).
RBAC (role-based) — permissions attach to job roles; users inherit their role's access.
Rule-based — global rules applied uniformly (e.g., time-of-day restrictions).
ABAC (attribute-based) — decisions from subject, resource, action, and environment attributes.
Always apply least privilege and revoke access promptly on role change or departure.

sections.heading: Cryptography basics
items: Symmetric (AES-256) — one shared key; fast; best for bulk data. Key distribution is the hard part.
Asymmetric (RSA, ECC) — public/private key pair; solves distribution; enables signatures. Slower.
Hashing (SHA-256) — one-way fixed-size digest; integrity checking, not encryption; cannot be reversed.
HMAC — hash plus a secret key for authenticated integrity.
Digital signature — hash encrypted with the sender's private key; proves authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation.
PKI/CA — certificate authorities bind public keys to identities; underpins TLS.
Encrypt with the recipient's PUBLIC key (confidentiality); sign with the sender's PRIVATE key (authenticity).

sections.heading: Backup types and recovery objectives
items: Full — everything; slowest to take, simplest to restore.
Incremental — changes since the last backup of any kind; fast backup, restore needs full + every incremental.
Differential — changes since the last full; restore needs full + latest differential only.
3-2-1 rule — 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite; keep one copy offline/immutable.
RTO — maximum tolerable downtime (drives recovery-site choice: hot/warm/cold).
RPO — maximum tolerable data loss in time (drives backup frequency).
BIA identifies critical processes; RTO never exceeds the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD).

sections.heading: CIA triad and risk formulas
items: Confidentiality — only authorized access (encryption, access controls, classification).
Integrity — accurate and altered only by authorized actions (hashing, signatures, change control).
Availability — reachable when needed (redundancy, backups, patching, DoS defenses).
Risk exists where a threat meets a vulnerability.
ALE = SLE x ARO. Implement a control when ALE reduction exceeds its annual cost.
Risk responses: reduce, transfer, accept, avoid. Risk is never eliminated.
Controls by function: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating. By category: administrative, technical, physical.

sections.heading: Network security quick map
items: L2: MAC flooding, ARP spoofing/poisoning (enables man-in-the-middle).
L3: IP spoofing, ICMP attacks. L4: SYN floods, port scans.
L7: phishing, SQL injection, XSS, DNS poisoning, malware delivery.
DMZ — screened subnet for public-facing services; databases stay internal.
IDS detects and alerts (passive); IPS blocks inline (active).
VPNs: site-to-site (IPsec, network to network); remote access (IPsec or TLS VPN, user to network).
Wireless: WEP is broken — never use; WPA3 (Enterprise + 802.1X) is current; evil twin = rogue AP impersonating the SSID; WIPS finds rogues.
